questions.title: Custom Validator - ConstraintValidator Interface
questions.question: How do you create a custom validator?

answer.summary: Create a custom validator by defining a constraint annotation (with @Constraint pointing to the validator class) and implementing ConstraintValidator<AnnotationType, FieldType> with an isValid() method containing your validation logic.

sections.title: When You Need Custom Validators
sections.content:
Built-in annotations cover common cases, but real applications need domain-specific validation. Is the phone number in a valid format for the user's country? Is the end date after the start date? Does the username contain only allowed characters? Does the product SKU follow your company's format?

Custom validators let you create your own annotations — like `@ValidPhoneNumber` or `@UniqueEmail` — that work exactly like the built-in ones. You annotate a field with your custom annotation, add `@Valid` on the request body, and the framework runs your validation logic automatically.

The process requires two pieces: the **constraint annotation** (the `@interface`) that defines the annotation itself, and the **validator class** (the `ConstraintValidator` implementation) that contains the actual logic.

sections.title: Building a Custom Validator
Cross-Field and Class-Level Validation
sections.content:
Some validations involve multiple fields — like checking that `endDate` is after `startDate`. You can't do this with field-level annotations because they only see one field. The solution is a **class-level validator**.

Instead of annotating a field, you annotate the entire DTO class: `@ValidDateRange public class EventRequest { ... }`. The validator receives the whole object and can access any field.

The validator class implements `ConstraintValidator<ValidDateRange, EventRequest>` and the `isValid()` method gets the full `EventRequest` object. You compare `startDate` and `endDate` directly.

Another powerful pattern is **injecting Spring beans into validators**. Since Hibernate Validator integrates with Spring's dependency injection, your validator can autowire repositories or services. A `@UniqueEmail` validator can inject `UserRepository` and check `existsByEmail()`. However, be cautious — this tightly couples validation to the database and can cause performance issues if validation triggers on every field change. Use database-backed validators sparingly and only for constraints that can't be checked any other way.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Two pieces required** — a `@Constraint` annotation (`@interface`) that links to a validator, and a `ConstraintValidator` class with the `isValid()` method
- **Return true for null values** — let `@NotNull` handle nullability separately; your validator should only check format/logic when a value is present
- **Class-level annotations for cross-field validation** — annotate the DTO class (not a field) when validation involves comparing multiple fields like start/end dates
- **Validators can inject Spring beans** — `@Autowired UserRepository` works in validators for database-backed checks like `@UniqueEmail`, but use sparingly for performance
- **Reusable across DTOs** — once created, `@ValidPhoneNumber` works on any field in any DTO; share validators across modules via a common library

Second, the **validator class** — it implements `ConstraintValidator<YourAnnotation, FieldType>` and overrides `isValid()`. This method contains your actual validation logic and returns true if valid, false if not.

A best practice is to **return true for null values** in your validator and let `@NotNull` handle nullability separately. This follows the principle that validators should only check what they're specifically about — format, range, or business rules.

For **cross-field validation** like "end date must be after start date," you create a class-level annotation that goes on the DTO class instead of a field. The validator then receives the entire object and can access multiple fields.

Since Spring integrates with Hibernate Validator, your validators can even **autowire Spring beans** — you could inject a `UserRepository` to check `@UniqueEmail`. But I use that sparingly because it couples validation to the database.

questions.title: @Validated vs @Valid - Method Level Validation
questions.question: What is the difference between @Validated and @Valid?

answer.summary: @Validated is Spring's extension of @Valid that adds support for validation groups (applying different constraints in different scenarios) and method-level validation on path variables and query parameters.

sections.title: Why Spring Created @Validated
sections.content:
Java's standard `@Valid` (from `jakarta.validation`) works well for simple cases — validate all constraints on a request body. But two scenarios need more:

**Validation groups** — Sometimes the same DTO is used for create and update operations, but the constraints differ. On create, all fields are required. On update, only the changed fields need validation. `@Valid` validates all constraints always; `@Validated` lets you select which group to apply.

**Method-level validation** — `@Valid` only works on method parameters annotated with `@RequestBody`. If you want to validate a `@PathVariable Long id` with `@Min(1)`, `@Valid` doesn't help. You need `@Validated` on the controller class to enable constraint annotations on individual method parameters.

sections.title: @Validated vs @Valid in Practice
Key Differences and When to Use Each
sections.content:
The distinction is straightforward: **use `@Valid` for standard request body validation** (the 90% case) and **`@Validated` when you need groups or method-level validation** (the 10% case).

`@Valid` is a **Java standard** (JSR-380, `jakarta.validation` package). It works in any Bean Validation implementation and triggers cascading validation on nested objects. It doesn't support groups.

`@Validated` is **Spring-specific** (`org.springframework.validation.annotation` package). It supports validation groups via `@Validated(OnCreate.class)` and enables method-level validation when placed on the class. However, it does not cascade into nested objects on its own — you still need `@Valid` on nested fields.

A common pattern is using both: `@Validated` on the controller class (for method-level validation) and `@Valid` on `@RequestBody` parameters (for request body validation). They're complementary, not competing.

One gotcha: when `@Validated` is on the class and a method-level constraint fails, Spring throws `ConstraintViolationException` — not `MethodArgumentNotValidException`. Your `@ControllerAdvice` needs to handle both exception types.

- **@Validated on the class enables method-level validation** — constraints on `@PathVariable` and `@RequestParam` only work when the controller class has `@Validated`
- **Method-level failures throw ConstraintViolationException** — different from `MethodArgumentNotValidException` thrown by `@Valid` on `@RequestBody`; handle both in your `@ControllerAdvice`
- **Use both together** — `@Validated` on the controller class for method params, `@Valid` on `@RequestBody` for request body validation; they complement each other

questions.title: Validation Groups - Conditional Validation
questions.question: What are validation groups?

answer.summary: Validation groups are marker interfaces that let you apply different constraints to the same DTO field depending on the operation. Assign constraints to groups, then specify which group to validate with @Validated(GroupName.class).

sections.title: The Problem Groups Solve
sections.content:
Consider a `UserRequest` DTO used for both creating and updating users. On **create**, you want `id` to be null (server generates it), `email` to be required, and `password` to be required. On **update**, `id` must be present, `email` is optional (only update if provided), and `password` isn't needed.

Without groups, you'd need separate DTOs: `CreateUserRequest` and `UpdateUserRequest`. With groups, a single DTO handles both — each constraint is tagged with the group(s) it belongs to, and the controller specifies which group to validate.

Groups are marker interfaces — empty interfaces with no methods. They exist purely as labels. `public interface OnCreate {}` and `public interface OnUpdate {}` are the conventions. You assign them via the `groups` attribute: `@NotNull(groups = OnCreate.class)`.

sections.title: Validation Groups in Action
Groups vs Separate DTOs
sections.content:
Validation groups aren't always the best approach. They add complexity — every team member needs to understand the group system, and it's easy to forget assigning a constraint to its groups.

**Use groups when** the create and update DTOs are nearly identical (80%+ field overlap) and the differences are small (a few fields required vs optional). This avoids duplicating a large DTO.

**Use separate DTOs when** the create and update payloads are fundamentally different, or when each DTO needs different field types (e.g., create accepts a password string, update doesn't have a password field at all). Separate DTOs are also clearer and easier for new team members to understand.

A constraint with **no group specified** belongs to the `Default` group. When you call `@Validated(OnCreate.class)`, only constraints in the `OnCreate` group run — `Default` group constraints are skipped. If you want both, the group interface must extend `Default`: `public interface OnCreate extends Default {}`. This is a common gotcha — suddenly your `@NotBlank` without a group stops working.

In practice, most teams prefer separate DTOs for clarity, and use groups only when the DTO duplication is truly excessive.

sections.content:
- **Groups are marker interfaces** — empty interfaces like `OnCreate` and `OnUpdate` used as labels on constraint annotations to control when they apply
- **Use `@Validated(GroupName.class)` to select a group** — only constraints tagged with that group are enforced; untagged constraints belong to the `Default` group
- **Extend `Default` to include ungrouped constraints** — `OnCreate extends Default` ensures constraints without explicit groups are still validated in the OnCreate context
- **Groups add complexity** — every constraint needs group assignment; prefer separate DTOs unless field overlap between create/update is very high (80%+)
- **Cannot use @Valid with groups** — `@Valid` always validates the `Default` group; only Spring's `@Validated` supports group selection

In practice, I only use groups when the **create and update DTOs overlap significantly**. If they're fundamentally different, separate DTOs are clearer and easier for the team to maintain. Groups add a layer of complexity that's only worth it when it prevents substantial code duplication.

questions.title: Validation Error Handling - MethodArgumentNotValidException
questions.question: How do you handle validation errors in Spring?

answer.summary: When @Valid fails, Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException. Catch it in @ControllerAdvice, extract field errors from BindingResult, and return a structured 400 response listing each field name, rejected value, and constraint message.

sections.title: How Validation Errors Flow in Spring
sections.content:
When a validation constraint fails, Spring doesn't just return a generic error — it builds a detailed `BindingResult` containing every field that failed, what value was submitted, and which constraint was violated. Your job is to catch the exception and format this information into a client-friendly response.

The exception type depends on where validation failed. **`@Valid` on `@RequestBody`** throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException`. **`@Validated` on the class for method params** throws `ConstraintViolationException`. These are different exception types with different structures — your error handler needs to handle both.

Without a custom handler, Spring's default response is a wall of text with a 400 status — technically correct but not useful for API consumers. A well-structured validation error response lists each failed field with its specific error message, letting the frontend highlight exactly which form fields need fixing.

sections.title: Handling Validation Errors in @ControllerAdvice
Best Practices for Validation Error Responses
sections.content:
**Return all errors at once**, not just the first one. If the name, email, and age are all invalid, the response should list all three. Making the user fix one field, resubmit, discover the next error, fix it, resubmit again — that's a terrible user experience. The `BindingResult` already collects all errors; just iterate over them.

**Include the rejected value** in the error response. When the error says "must be a valid email" and the rejected value is "john.doe", the user immediately sees they forgot the @domain part. Without the rejected value, they have to remember what they typed.

**Sort field errors** in the same order as the form fields. If the form shows name, email, age from top to bottom, the error list should follow the same order. This helps frontend developers display errors next to the right fields.

**Handle both exception types**. `MethodArgumentNotValidException` from `@Valid` on `@RequestBody` and `ConstraintViolationException` from `@Validated` on method parameters have different APIs. Both should produce the same response format so clients don't need two different error parsers.

**Don't expose field paths that leak internals**. If your DTO has `addressDto.zipCode` but the form field is labeled "ZIP Code", map the field path to the frontend's expected name.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`MethodArgumentNotValidException` for @RequestBody** — thrown when `@Valid` validation fails; contains `BindingResult` with all field errors and rejected values
- **`ConstraintViolationException` for method params** — thrown when `@Validated` class-level validation fails on `@PathVariable`/`@RequestParam` constraints
- **Return ALL errors at once** — iterate the full `BindingResult`, don't stop at the first failure; users shouldn't have to submit repeatedly to find all problems
- **Include field name, message, and rejected value** — `{"field":"email","message":"must be valid","rejectedValue":"bad"}` tells the client exactly what to fix
- **Handle both exception types with the same response format** — clients should see identical error structures regardless of whether the failure was in the body or a path variable
